The favorable prospects of an abundant crop in this Ialand in 1862, forces the attention of our planters toward the insufficient means at the r command for working their Estates and reaping the full benefit of the favors bestowed upon them by Providence. We have consequently of late seen a revival ol the discussions upon the matter of immigration, and the minds of our leading planters are now seriously engaged upon this all-important subject. It is certainly not an hour too early, and we trust it may not he too late ; for it is obvious to all, and it is confirmed bv our experience from the present not unusually large crop, that not only will tiie reaping of a crop as large as the one expected, be extremely difficult, hut that moreover it will be next to impossible to attend to the raising of a succeeding crop. Admitting this, that our we think indisputable, let us sincerely hope which planters will bestir themselves in earnest, that they will not allow their ardour to be damped, but will proceed at once to action, without more less of a most invaluable time; for the time is indeed already Very short in which to secure additional bib t for raising the crop of 1863, say from now till ;iext. spring and not a moment thereof should be \va fi d. And let us at once add, that in our opinion, j i t' tors had bc.-t take the matter into their own hands, a d act by them selves and for themselves ; "aide toi, et le ciel t'aidera" is the truest saying of a clever people, and truly our

planters will find it so. Our Governm t will certainly assist them to the extent of some dispatches and diplomatic notes, and, it is said « it it li would loan, but not one whit further; and $15,000 as a he regretful to see a most precious time h>st in waiting for more material help from Government Even, if they might make a show of willingness to do more for its, it must be remembered that the Danish Governmentmachine is the most complicated one in the world; and ere any proposed measure would have passed through its prescribed course of debates belorc two political bodies here, and uvo at home, besides the iocal-Govermnent and the home-Government, the useful tinio will have slipped away, and the failure in securing a timely reaping of next ciop together with the establishing of that of 1863, will in all probability carry with it the impossibility for planters in ubsequently raising the necessary means toward an immigration, whereas new, such means will no doubt be forthcoming upon the anticipation of a large crop near at hand. These views have led us to reflect seriously upon the manner in which we should set to work for attain, ing the desired purpose within the shortest possible time; and the result of our reflections is, that the course now about to be taken by our planters, namely by petitioning tlie local-Government to move the liome- Grvernment to conclude a treaty with Groat Britain for the concession of a Coolie-emigration from Bengal, in the same manner as the treaty lately concluded

will by no means prove the shortest nor the quickest. Not to mention the known disinclination ol the Danish Government to the residence here of a British official, which, however, will probably vanish after some tune, that Government is proverbially slow of action, especially so in its diplomatic negotiations with foreign rowers. The British Government will to all certainty find an obstacle in our labor-regulations, and particularly in the fixed wages ordained therein, and whatever they may ultimately resolve, and whether they give way, or the labor act is to be first repealed, at least in part, there is a moral certainty of considerable delays before any such treaty will be concluded. Now, under ordinary circumstances, such delays would not be very inconvenient, for everybody knows the slow and solemn routine of diplomatic negotiations, and that there is no means of pressing them on ; but in our case delay is fatal, and must, if possible, be evaded. VVc do not mean by the above remarks in any way to disparage, or even to undervalue, the measures about to be adopted by our planters ; they are in themselves good and a step in the right direction. But they are not sufficient, tliey warrant no hopes of our being immediately saved from impending ruin; and though, if successful, they do promise to be beneficial to us if we survive till then, yet we must at once look for other means besides, to enable us to save ourselves, and to live to reap the fruits of the aimed-at treaty. There-

fore, by tho sideof this intended measure, which should proceed on its course, we would propose that steps be at once taken for an immigration of Chinese. !n China, as is notorious, we meet w ith no difficul ties from its Government, or its local Authorities, in fact, we have no concern with its reigning powers. We meet with a teeming population of hardy and industrious laborers, who desire nothing bettor, tlian to leave their own overpeopled country for a more remunerative field ot labor. By all accounts we have seen, the Chinese laborers work better than the Coolies, and they engage their labor for a longer term than these, besides which they do not stipulate for a free returnpassage, like the Coolies These advantages must, in out opinion fully counterbalance the lesser cost at which Coolies can be placed here, and when, as we know, no time has to be lost in negotiations, or in asking permission, or in palavering with this consul or that official, but that one has, so to say, only to receive the people who offer themselves, make the contracts with them, and find a vessel in which to ship them here, we should think it most recommendable to our

TF « ft I 9, U AVI j $«. planters to turn at once to this source of immigration. In following this course, tiiey will meet with no diplomatic difficulties, and with no delays, and to those who would uphold our labor-act it will be a consolation to know, that a Chinese immigration can take place without necessitating any change hi t1 e regulations We will not here enter into the detail of the relations connected with a Chinese immigration, they can be discussed at a meeting of planters, if such he their pleasure. But we would urge an immediate proceeding to action in the matter, and we would recommend to the planters to use decision, promptitude and energy. Their best course would undoubtedly b to send an Agent from here to carry out their aim and to accelerate the immigration, passing first to England, in order there to settle all necessary preliminary arrangements. Such an Agent wouid have no other business on hand, and could therefore employ all his energies upon, as well as give all his time to the one business entrusted tn him, without being trammeled by any of the considerations which so often influence the actions of those, wlio at the same time act as Agents toother parties. The cost would probably not be more, than it would be by employing an English Agent resident in China ; but even it otherwise, we opine that a trifl more or a trifle less is of sina.l cons quence compared to tho saving of time that will in all likelihood he gained by liav.n" an Agent ol our own, who has to and for us only, and to consult our interests alone, act
who therefore will inake speed his principal aim. St. Croix, 28th August 1861.

COMMUNICATION. St. Croix, 2nd September 1861. To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis, Dear Sir, It is remarkable what a degree of presumption some persons can assume, and this circumstance cannot be more forcibly illustrated than in the reply to my communication to you, of 22ud ult., (respecting tlioro being, at present, no proper vestry in St. John's Church) by Mr. James Brown, who has taken it upon himself, to state, that had I ''taken the pains to obtain proper " information" regarding what I wrote you about, by applying in the right quarter 1 could have got it." Pray, Air. Editor, which quarter shall I apply to for information, as he omitted to direct me to a definite quarter, and I might be running a "wild-goose-chase," from tlio hind quarter to the fore quarter, from the East quarter to the 11m< quarter þÿ and still not find the right quarter. Please desire him fo direct me definitely to the right quarter, and mention to him, that as a private individual he can give me the sought for information, but in an official capacity he can no longer act legally, as he is hut one sixth part of the vestry of St. John's Church; which, consisting now only of two members, can no longer act legally in any case, two not being a quorum of six. Respectfully, An Enquirer. a CHRIST! ANSTED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 3rd SEPTEMBER, 1S61

We have been requested by parties in this Island, subscribers to the "St. Thorn® Tidende,' to draw the attention of the publisher of that paper to the irregular manner in which their copies are received hete. Yesterday morning only three subscribers received that paper for Saturday, viz: those who subscribe through the Post Office ; while those who pay postage on each single number received no copies. The publisher, we remember, has on a previous occasion informed us that he places all the copies for this place in the Post Office simultaneously ; consequently it is to the Post Office that wo fear the blame must be attached. Whether the Postmaster in St. Thomas docs not consider himself bound to forward every newspaper or letter by the first opportunity, is a question which we leave to the authorities to decide: on our part all wc can state is that the postago on that paper, amounting as it does to over S3 yearly, is not so inconsiderable a sura that the rights of the subscribers here to receive their papers in proper time should bo altogether left to the whim of tho Postmaster.

The Tiglif ,\ear Springfield. The following is an official report of the fight near Springfield on Saturday, forwarded by one of Gen. Lyon's aids : þÿ To Major-General Fremont: Gen. Ly< n in three columns, under himself, Gen. Siegel and Maj. Sturgis, attacked the enemy at 6£ o'clock on the morning of the 10th, nine miles southeast of Springfield. The engagement was severe. þÿ Our loss is about 800 in killed and wounded. General Lyon was killed in a charge at the head of his column. Our force was 8,000, including 2,000 Ilome Guards. The muster rol's tukeD from the enemy give his force as 23,900, including regiments from Louisiana, Mississippi, Tennessee, Texas Rangers, and Cherokee half breeds. Their loss is reported heavy, including Generals McCulloch and Piice. This statement is corroborated by prisoners. þÿ Their tents and waggons were destroyed in the action. Gen. Siegel left, only one gun on the field. Ho retreated to Springfield with a large number of prisoners. At 3 o'clock on the morning of the 11th, he continued his retreat on Rolla bringing off bis baggage trains and 825, COO in specie from the Springfield banks. The following is the verbatim report of lie special messenger to Gen. Fremont : " Early on Saturday morning General Lyon marched out of Springfield. He canto up with the enemy on Davis Crock, on Green's Prairie, four miles southwest of Springfield, where they had taken a strong position. Gen. Lyon fired the first gun at 20 minutes past 6 when tho battle immediately began. A severe cannon-

ading was kept up two or three hours, when the fire of Tottcn's artillery becoming too severe for the enemy they gradually fell back towards their encampment on Wilson's Creek. Gen. Lyon's cavalry on their left hand, and General Siegel's artillery on tho right, then began a terrific attack, and spread slaughter and dismay in the ranks of the rebels, pursuing them to their canips. The shells from Totten's artillery set fire to their tents and baggage wagons, which were all destroyed. A Louisiana and a Mississippi regiment seemed to suffer the most, and were almost annihilated. Some time in the afternoon, while Gen. Lyon was leading his column, his horse was shot under him. Immediately he mounted another and as he turned round to his men, waving bis hat and cheering his men on to victory, he was struck in the small of his back and fell load to tho ground. The command then devolved on Gen. Siege! þÿ The pursuit was continued until nightfall when our little army rested for the night in the enemy's encampment. Sunday morning, Gen. Sicgel, fearing the enemy might recover and attempt to cut his command oft' from Sprinficld fell back on that city, where the Home Guards were stationed. Then fearing the great numbers of the enemy might induce tbem to get between him and Rolla, Gen. Sicgel concluded to fall back on Rolla with his provision train, and meet reinforcements. At the time of the departure of the messenger the enemy had not been seen, nnd it is probable that Gen. Siegel was not disturbed on his march .

Ninety rebels were captured, including a colonel of distinction, the messenger not remembering bis name. Tho sword and horse of Gen. McCulloch were among tho trophies. Reinforcements are on the way to Rolla, and Gen. Siegel and his army may be considered safe. Cairo, 13 th. The Secretary of War has addressed an important letter to General Butler respecting the disposition of fugitive slaves set king protection at his hands, lie states that it is the desire of the President that all existing rights in all the States be fully respected and maiutaincd. Tbo war now prosecuted on the part of the federal government is a war for the Union, for tho preservation of all constitutional rights of States, and the citizens of tho States in the Uuion. Hence no question can arise as to fugitives from service within tho States and Territories in which the authorities of tho Uuion is fully acknowledged. But he says that iu the States wholly or in part under insurrectionary coutrol, where tho laws of the United States are so fur opposed and resisted that they cannot bo effectually enforced, it is obvious that the rights depeudent upon the execution of those laws must temporarily fail, and if is equally obvious that the rights dependent on the laws of the State within which military operations are conducted must be necessarily subordinate to the exigencies created by tho insurrection, if not wholly forfeited by tho treasonable conduct of parties claiming them. To tliis the general rule of right to services forms an exception. The act of Congross approved August 1861 declares that in if persons held to scrvico shall he employed hostility to the United States, the right to their

T . C If U i A V I S , service shall he forfeited and such persons shall be discharged therefrom. It follows, he adds, of necessity that no claim can bo recognized by the military authority of the Uuion for the services of such persons when fugitives. With respect to the slaves of loyal masters, Mr. Cameron says that a careful record should he kept of the name and description of such fugitives, in order that Congress may provide for a just compensation for their services when peace is restored. Gen. Butler is instructed not to permit any interference by his troops with the slaves of peaceful citizens, nor encourage them to leave the service of their masters nor prevent the voluntary return of any fugitives to those from whom they may have escaped.

The following correspondence between a merchant in Liverpool and Mr. At Burtis of New York, regarding the political state of the United Stales, a copy of which has been kindli lent us for puhiication, we take this opportunity to lay before our readers, in the hope that it might prove of some interest. Ill doing so, we must, however, state that we do not endorse the opinion of Mr. Al Hurl is on t ie w hole, for there is much that can he said in justification of the course adopted by tho Southern States In our next, we will lav before our readers an article from a London Paper, which takes quite a different view of the matter than that taken by Mr. Al Burtia. Liverpool , 4th May, P. M. 1861. Saturday A/Urnoon,
E. K. Al BURTIS, Esq. New-York. Dear Sir. þÿ The Persia's news reached here this morning, and created a most fearful sensation as it will do every-

where else. It is not only sad, but shocking, not to say wicked and everything that is bad, to think that the United States (alas! no longer united) can have come to such a pass. People here grieve over it. We don't know a soul who feels otherwise than sorrow the most profound, at such a spectacle as that being enacted in America. The writer's sympathies, he at once admits, are all with the South and Southern men. He has no sympathy with those who would oppress the Southern man and his property, and he prophecies, at starting, that in actual war the North will be beaten, and the South become "de facto," as well as " de jure," a nation of themselves þÿ free, liberal, anti-monopoly, and anti-tariff people þÿ and he deeply regrets a separation was not quietly acquiesced in by the Lincoln Administration, (w liich by prudent counsels might have easily and well have arranged all matters,) and thus though amicably separated they would never have been politically disunited þÿ whereas, now, the bundle of sticks can no longer exist. It is a sad business, and may God defend the right! You are at liberty to make known these sentiments. Sic. & c &.c. Yours, Si. c.

Liverpool. Dear Sir : þÿ I have received your letter of the 4th May, and am much obliged by your advices respecting cotton, the true position of which at the present moovnt, (to judge from the course of your market,) Liverpool, evidently, but imperfectly comprehends. Yon do not seem to appreciate the fact that our Government does not exist by sufferance of either alien or domestic enemies, and therefore you appear to think, you will get hereafter your usual supply of cotton from tiiis side. You seem to regard the constituted authorities at Washington, as enacting a grand force for the diverlisement of innocent spectators not directly interested, and that they wouid not have the heart to inconvenience any one. You do not seem to un ierstand that our Government has ordered the closing of the Southern ports and that the export of cotton may be s effectually stop|>ed as if the ports were hermetically scaled. You do not seem to understand that from this time dates the Second Epoch of Concitutioual Liberty, for which the present struggle is life or death. These and various other reasons do not seem apparent to you, and it may take some time for you to realise, what you must, in the future know. I would be content to confine my remarks to cotton, and could extend them further on that subject; but as your letter is principally made up of your views of the present troubles in which this country is involved, I should fear lest I might be considered as holding the same opinions you express, if I did not definitely refute them,

and say to yon, in the most emphatic manner, you have mistaken your mm. You say you sympathise with " Southern men and the South: to do this in your position, as a passive sympathiser can do no harm ; but it may be wi ll for you, not to let your sympathies so lead you into error as to force you to conclude that "the North will be beaten in actual war, an I the South will become a nation, free, libera1, anti-monopoly, and anti tariff." and you might have added anti-payers of debts. Under what delusion can you rest when you express such hopes of a nationality founded (if ever) on such a basis as would be the so-called Southern Confederacy ? In the place of your word " free" you must substitute slave, for " liberal," insolent, for " anti-monopoly," States peopled bv millions of slaves owned in life and death by a few, and for "anti-tariff" I will not attempt a substitute as it is in that view and the prospect of short supplies of cotton that your sympathies and those of some of your country-men, as clearly indicated by the course of a portion of your press may be captivated ; and you show your willingness to sacrifice on your part, those high principles under which alone nations can exist. Some of the people of your nation seem not yet to have learned that the expression of an opinion, ignorant of its subject is not yet current every where, or I am satisfied we should have been spared the insulting advice so freely given to let our country be divided and our liberties stolen. I contend that ignorance alone

can excuse such presumption. What would you havo thought of me, if in 1857, I should have written to you, I strongly sympathised with the Sepoys of India, &c. &.c. And in what respect have their atrocities against your government been exceeded by the traitors against this ? Aye, rather it is in the Sepoys' favor, for they were fighting to recover their Country, their Liberty, and their Religion ; while our Rebels are attempting to destroy all : þÿ Country, Liberty, Religion and Justice, and seek to set up in the place of the fairest Government on earth, an oligarchical slaveocracy, founded on the magnitude of its injustice, and the remorselessness of its cruelty. Yet you in justice-loving England, so sympathise ; and wherefore ? Cotton ! ! ! If cotton is to override every principle of justice and truth, would it not have been well for your people, before setting up as exemplars for the rest of the World, to have considered more fully the value of the staple.

T-. Cr s ® I I f V I » You say that the " bundle of sticks" is separated ; that may, in your case, be a wish " father to the thought;" but you forget that the withes that bind them are heir-looms of our forefathers, consecrated by their blood þÿ that the ties that have held this country together have been made from the eternal principles of Liberty and Justice, devoted love toward and admiration for our country, and a deep reverence, and abiding reliance on our God Such are the people who are to uphold our Constuution and Laws, and it is such a people you expect to see abandon their mand of the lord of cotton. This " bundle of sticks," all at the comas you have chosen to typify my country, the world will ere long know, nre bound together by freemen's will and freemen's might, both of which are pledged to the last, to uphold the constitutionally installed authorities in defending our whole country from either internal or external eu.mies, and t at those in arms against these authorities must either conquer us or succumb. I pray you, my friend, consider if there be not higher principles, and more vital for a nation to regard than the price of cotton. Do you think the Southern Rebellion would ever have raised its serpent head so high, had not the astute minds of their leaders in treason have counted fully upon the value of their staple, and upon forcing even England into supporting their beloved institution (slavery) ? Aye, froud England! to uphold slavery, and force her to give the lie to all her professions and acts for the last forty

þÿyears, forcing her to advocate the vilest lorm of despotism and for cotton! !! No, Sir; I have often been a sojourner in your fair land, I know well the sentiments there, and have suffered many a taunt, even in Manchester, lor coming from a country where the poor black man was bound in chains : I have often questioned the sincerity of those most exercised on the subject ; hut still 1 have seen enough to know it will be ! flt Coiniteen ikke vilde have an impossibility for England to take any part or int in our struggle. The people of the country will not permit it. We do not fear the result; we have perfect confidence in our cause ; we know our strength; we believe in our right, and we will detend it with our lives. No interference of any kind will he tolerated, and on this you may rely, we stand or fall a great and undivided nation. The tune of patching and compromising is past; the slave power, in tins country, has tried to snatch away our liberties; they have corrupted our people; they have proved tliem-elves incapable of understanding or tolerating con.-titutio al liberty; therefore that power must be curtailed; yes, broken, if not altogether alii- Inlated. We can no longer look upon the South as representing a slave interest, as has heretofore been the case in our national councils ; that idea can nev r again be tolerated; they may retain their slaves, but the political element of slavery, is doomed and dead ; and it is my opinion that slavery itself has heard its death knell. And th n, say you, what is to become

of the poor slave ? That may be answered by referring you to the fate of the captive when contended for by rival superior forces. I hope for thein a better fate; but still, thirty millions of white people cannot he continually cutting each«otliers's throats about four millions of biacks; the latter must be got rid of, and may the most humane means practicable be adopted to that end is my earnest wish. On whatever occasion heretofore I have exercised my right of franchise, or attempted political influence, it lias been on the side of the South; for t1 at reason, you will see I am no philanthropic abolitionist; but I new wish to see my country freed from slavery, on the ground that my own liberties are iti danger. I have had full opportunity to see and understand some of the treachery and baseness of Southern politicians, towards their political friends here, and I am thoroughly convinced of their wickedness and enmity to constitutional liberty. You then ask, why not let them go? Toe same question will apply to your country, why did you not let Ireland go? I will tell you, they are too near, and too antagoni-tic in both cases. Among all our apparent follies, do not think we are sufficiently demented to raise up a power so entirely opposed to all the principles of human progress as would be the socalled Southern Confederacy, and expect from them friendship and neighborly conduct, whilst we maintained our Constitution and Laws, founded upon principles exactly the reverse of those on which the slave piwer

pretends to stand. How long would these people remain at peace? Just long enough for the slave power to consolidate its strength. To them war would be pastime; þÿ to us, destruction. If the South, the North, the East, or the West cannot exist under our present Constitution, it is not Republic liberty they want; it is universal slavery, or military despotism, and all their attendant horrors. Nay, friend, you may rest assured we will never permit ourselves to fall into this trap. Now to close: and with a word for that country of which I am so justly proud; it was hero that Liberty was born : it was here that mankind first learned to understand his kindred, and believe them capub'e of trust ; it is from here that ail the reforms of Const, tutional Libprty throughout the world have been taken; it was here that the tyrant's sway was first disputed, and his sceptre broken ; it was here that the man on whom all European eyes now look with wonder perfected his ideas of liberty ao as to enable hnn to free his nation, which had been bound in chains for a thousand years; and it was hpre that he could learn to appreciate, that a nation's love, was more to he prized than a tyrant's caressea: and it is to this point that the down-trodden masses of Europe, turn their longing eyea for sympathy, and to them, and to our-
þÿ selves, we owe the obligation to maintain God's first gift to man, Liberty. I remain Yours truly, E. K. ALBURTIS

l CHRIST1ANSTED, ST. CROIX TUESDAY, 23UD JULY 1861. THE LAST MEETING of tbc Colonial Council was held to day The Reports to His Majesty fiom 'lie Council on several Drufts Were read. His Excellency the Governor then addressed the Ass. mbly and observed, that scarcely in any foregoing session of the Colonial Council have more motions telating to matteis of vast impoitance for the Colonies been brougb' forward, than in the one that was about to be closed. Among the motions brought forward by Government he mentioned : 1st, The Plan for effecting a reduction of the military forces in these Islands, hy which, notwithstanding an improvement in the pecuniary situation of the the proposed, there will, for Officers has bceu future, be obtained a saving of at least $12000 in the 2ndly. The Plan for effecting the Island's expenses for these Colonies ; the diffe rential duty on this abolition f pro- . duce, when expoited to foreign places ; 3dly. The Proposal of changing the variable export-duty on S'. Croix pioduee to a moderate fixed export-duty. The following proposals, ho i etna iked, have " been made by the Council : 1st. The abolition of the d.fferciit exceptions hitherto grautcd hy the Custom Laws of the Island in favor of goods imported from the Mother Country in Danish vessels, and in connection therewith a veiy considerable reduction in the export-duty on sugar ; 2dly. The division of the Colonial Council in two separate Assemblies, the one lor St. Croix, the other for St Thomas aud St. Johns ; 3dly. The separation of the finances of St.

Croix from those of the Mother Countiy. These were the 6 most important mallei s, that have occupied the Council during the Session ; but it must be borne iu mind, that the two first mentioned ones are to be considerid only as the conclusion of discussions on the same matters in previous Sessions of the Council; that the third one can be regaidcd as a continuation from a new side ol the de iberations on a matter tbat was first touched on in the last Session, and that the tbiee others arc en'iiely new matters, now for the first time brought forward in the Council. It is not to be wondered at then, that the fate of these diffeieut motions, even wl ile tliey were being discussed in the Council, has been very different. The reduction of the military forces to the extent as proposed by Government has met no opposition at all, and the same is the case with regard to the abolition of the differential export-duty ; but as r. gards the third motion, which in this form has first now been brought in the Council, the manner in which the Government has proposed to realize the plau has met wiih obj. ctions ; and iu p.oceeding to the 3 lust-mentioned motions, it will be found, that the opinions and votings in the Council have been divided, just in proportion to the importance of the questions involved in the matters. It would have been unnatuial had it beeo otherwise. It is only through discussion, and by being regarded from different points of view, that plans relating to changes of great importance san be duly aud fully devel-

oped. It did not rest with him nor was it in his power to foretell the final result, which tlieso matters will have ; but he would lose no time in forwarding the Reports of the Counc 1 to the Home Government to be laid before His Majesty. His Excellency then expressed his thanks to the honorable members of -the Council lor the assiduity :aod promptitude, with which they have attended the meetings, aud expressed his acknowledgment of the good zeal showu hy the honorable Chairman and the honorable Secretary. Finally the Governor in the name of His Majesty declared the fifth Session of the Colonial Council closed. From the St. Thomas Times, July 17. Our readers have no doubt read with interest the Draft introduced into the Colonial Council (St. Croix) to erect a separate

t , a & 1 1 x a. <1. s , Council for this Island. The period that has intervened since this community endeavoured, with much zeal, to secure a separate Council is so hug, that it may, in the first instance, demand some public ex- j erf ion before the community wi 1 1 again be. aroused to reconsider, with sufficient importance, the nature of what it is now proposed to bestow upon the Island. It is, of course, only a Draft, that may meet with j such overwhelming opposition somewhere, as to preclude it after all becoming a law ; y« t this we do not believe, as it is in reality already so by the 1st of the Colonial Law. We may, therefore, take it for granted that alter a while this Island will be called upon to elect eight members to preside in a Council, for the purpose of consulting over such questions as may effect the good or evil of the place. It would tlierelore be well tint every one who, by position, will have to play some part therein, to think the matter over, and i not make light of what, by neglect, may prove to his cost in the end. Of all things let there be consistency ; let not those who at first advocated a separate Council, | because, may be, they thought there would be none, now ask what do we want with a Council? For let it not be forgotten that we shall now have to deal with a fact, that just in proportion as it is dealt with earnestly and seriously, so will it produce its fruits. It has heretofore been the common practice of all oegrees of society, whether openly or one to another, to grumble about

the Government, and to attach blame, whether real or imaginary, to it for whatever transpired. L. Petersen. Fm. Publication from the Ministry of Finances, dated the 30th of June 1861, whereby the Ordinance of 4th May 1803 is again put in force in the Danish Westindia Possessions. His Majesty the King has under date of the 29th of this month most graciously authorised the Ministry of Finances to remind all his Majesty's subjects in the Danish Westindia Possessions of the rules contained in the Ordinance of 4th May 1803, and at the same time to make known, that owing to the warlike disturbances at present taking place in the United States, the said Ordinance will again be put in force in every part of His þÿMajesty West- s india Possessions from the day this Publication has been promulgated there. The Ministry of Finances, pursuant to His þÿMajesty s command, furthermore makes known and impresses the following rules : $ 1. Instead of the Royal Latin ca- Passport prescribed in the Ordinance of 4th May J 03 vessels belonging to the Danish Westmoa Possessions will, as hitherto, have to provide themselves with the prescribed Westindia Sea- Passport for voyages between the Danish Westindia Islands as likewise to all places in the Westindies and America ; the said Sea- Passport in the latter case not, however, for being issued for any number of months, bur. for every single voyage, stating those places which it is the intention of the vessel to touch at during the voyage. Should circumstances make further regulations necesssary to prevent abuses of the danish flag, the Government of the Danish West-

india Possessions is hereby authorized to give provisional enactments in this respect, in such case it will be incumbent on the masters of vessels to procure such proofs of nationality, as might eventually be required besides the Westindia Sea- Passport. $ 2. Besides the articles enumerated in Article 13 of the Ordinance of 4th May 1803 all such manufactured articles, that according to the art of war of the present day are directly applicable for warlike purposes are to be considered a contraband of war. The foregoing is hereby made known for the information and observance of all concerned. The Ministry of Finances, Copenhagen, the 30th of June 1861. FENGER.
L. Petersen.

St. Croix. 13th August 1861. Admiral Sir Alexander Milne and the Blockade of the Southern Ports.

A letter from Fort Pickens, dated July 15 has the following A British steam frigate has arrived here from Havana, and is now swinging from a pair of anchors The the Sabine. in the berth occupied by officer in command of the former vessel makes no secret of bis mission. It is, be says, to see that the rights ol English commerce are protect! d; and that the blockade must be such as will prevent " the entrance or departure of any craft to or from any harbor of the South, coaster, ocean trailer or tender." This will be strange intelligence to the majority of laid readers. 'The treaty of Paris has not our down any rules by which we may know what is and what is not an effective blockade. Admiral Milne makes up for the deficiency. Here is his definition as comman- ed to one of his subordinate furnishders : þÿ

1. No port is blockaded efficiently if any vessel can enter or depart from it unknown to, or in spite of, the guardian menof-war. 2. An efficient blockade necessitates the complete cutting oil' of all maritime ingress or egress, except in regard to harbor islands, having no outlet to the sea, save under the guns of the fleet. 3. The escape of the third vessel from the blockading squadron signalizes the invalidity of the blockade. " Under the latter rule" pays the New York Times of the 13th instant, " the Blockade of New-Orleans, even by the confession of our own Naval officers, who are maintaining at the mouths of the Mississippi a nominal surveillance is invalid, mav be declared so by Admiral Milne, and involves us in a difficulty little anticipated, but calculated to exert a most disastrous influence upon the present contest. A thorough and effectual blockade would in time utterly destroy the rebels. But England is as much interested in raising it as we are in maintaining it. It has never been believed there that we could make t lie blockade effectual, and the instructions from the Admiral have undoubtedly been prepared upon such a supposition. We have no doubt that Mr. Muir, the British Consul at New-Orleans, whose business it is to discover any loophole through wuicli the shipment of cotton to Liverpool may he resumed, lias a list ready for his Admiral of twenty vessels that have run I lie blockade since we assumed to make it a competent one. The evidence may he so conclusive that we ourselves may

be compelled to acknowledge its force, although an attempt to raise the blockade would, under any circumstances, inevitably lead to a war with England. Here is a matter d 'sprving the most careful attention of our Government. England has vast interests at stake in opening the Southern ports. Upon it may depend the empl oyment of millions of operatives as well as commercial revulsion, which may overwhelm that country with ruin. Every legal defect in our panc.eeding will be taken advantage of. To have our blockade broken would he equivalent to the loss of a campaign. It would supply the enemy with what it now lacks þÿ means for prosecuting the war on a gram! scale It would destroy the prestige we have been steadily gaining and perhaps engage us in a foreign as well as a domestic war. It would help to turn loose a swarm of pirates upon our commerce Wo ' cannot, indeed, imagine a condition of things more fraught with danger every aspect than an ineffi- in cient blockade of such a port as New-Orleans. Will the Government take immediate steps to avert the threatened peril, and restore public confidence? It is absolutely essential that we wield that great arm, our Navv, in a manner to secure respect abroad and protection at home, and destroy the tebels by destroying their means of existence." þÿ Bermuda Ri val Gazette.

THE BATTLE; 1--A- .11 .u no\. The bat tie so long promised by the Americans, which was to astonish the world, has conio off at last. The Federal army, under General McDowell, encountered the secessionists, commanded by General Johnson, at the Manassas Junction, where, if we can rely upon the teletook place, risulting in graphic rep rt, a most the sanguinary engagement defeat of the Federal troops with a loss of between four and five thousand men killed, besides a vast number wounded. We have no account of the number of killed and wounded on the Confederate side, but if it has any proportion to the Federal loss, the battle of Manassas may fairly lay claim to have been odb of the most bloody on record, exceeding in destruction of life, in proportion to

the number engagi d, the most disastrous engagements of modern times þÿ the battles of Inkerman and Solferino It is not, perhaps, reasonable to suppose that the amount of the Federal loss, comiugasit does, through Northern sources, is at all magnified ; the error, if any, might naturally be looked for the other way ; still we caiiuot help thinking there must be some mistake, an exaggeration of loss on the part of the reporters lor the press, who may possibly have shared the panic which is said to have seized that portion of the army which took to their heels and run away. Five thousand killed out of filty thousand engig, d, is a frightful amount of carnage, scaicely possible uuder the circumstances, and which we will hesitate to believe until the official accounts <joine to hand. One thing, however, is certain. The Northern troops have suffeied a most crushing defeat on a field of battle selected by themselves. At the last accounts they were in full retreat on Washington, whither it was supposed the Southem aimy would follow them, with the view of seizing on the capital. However much the Secessionists may be flushed with victory, we do not believe that they will attempt any aggressive movement. We believe it to he the polioy of their leaders, as at ihe Manassas Junction, to pin sue a defensive policy þÿ to wait until they are attacked in t heir strongholds, where, armed with equal, if not superior force, the chances of vicio.y will always be on their side. There can

be uo doubt that the Federal army fought at great disadvantage. The Southerners were on their owu soil, and besides being familiar with every part of the grouud, had, it is said, the b> nefit of entrcncliuieuts and masked batteries, from which a deadly fiie was poured fourth on the attacking force. They had also, it is believed, the advantage of being better officered" and more thoroughly disciplined than the Federalists, and when to this it is added that the Southern aimy was nearly double that of the Federalis's, we cannot wonder that the latter were signally d> leated Our surprise is that Gi ii. Seott risked an engagement under such citcuinstaiices ; and we cannot help thinking that t lie cautious old General, besides being deceived as to the real strength of the t uemy, has jielded to public clamour, aud fought a battle, tor which he was not prepared, coutrary to his own judgment. We call imagine the effect of this battle on the minds of the Noithern people, who were persuaded that General Seott had the gamo entirely in Lis own hands, and that lie was steadily unrounding i he enemy, eDcircling them in a lot fiom which there was no escape. All these high hopes and expectations have been suddenly da.-lied to the ground, and Jefferson Davis, in-tcad of being trapped, is master of the p sition We have no doubt that the Federal Government will make a desperate effort to retiicve their los-, but tliey have a hard task to perforin. The Secessionists appear to be ably officered, united, and enthusiastic in battling for

their indi p ndctice. The Federal army is certainly not wed led, and, il we can rely on the telegrams, abounds witli "traitors,'' who issue "lame orders" and create "panic" iu the troops under i heir command. We await with somo anxiety the next movent! nt of the Federal army, which lor weal or lor woe, must necessarily exercise a laige influence on ibe i.-sue of the campaign. Publication from the Ministry of Finances, dated the 30tli of June 1861, whereby the Ordinance of 4th May 1803 is again put in force in the Danish Westiadia Possessions. II is Majesty the King has under date of the 29th of this month most graciously authorised the Ministry of Finances to remind all his Majesty's subjects in tbe Danish Westindia Possessions of the rules contained in the Ordinance of 4th May 1803, and at the same time to make known, that owing to the warlike disturbances at present taking place in the United States, the said Ordinance will again be put in force in every part of His Majesty's Westindia Possessions from the day this Publication has been promulgated there. 'I he Ministry of Finances, pursuant to makes Majesty's command, furthermore His known and impresses the following rules : 1. Instead of the Royal Latin ea- Passport prescribed in the Ordinance of 4tli May 1803 vessels belonging to the Danish Westimlia Possessions will, as hitherto, have to providfe themselves with lor the prescribed Westindia Sea- Passport voyages between the Danish Westindia Islands as likewise to all places in the Westindies and America; the said Sea- Passport in the latter case not, however, for being issued for any number of months, bur tor every single voyage, stating those places which it is the intention of the vessel to touch at during the voyage. Should circumstances make further regulations necessary to prevent abuses of the danish flag, the Government of the Danish West-

india Possessions is hereby authorized to give provisional enactments in this respect, in such case it will be incumbent on the masters of vessels to procure such proofs of nationality, as might eventually be required besides the Westindia Sea- Passport. 2' Besides the articles enumerated in Article 13 of the Ordinance of 4th May 1803 all such manufactured articles, that according to the art of war of the present day are directly applicable for warlike purposes are to be considered a contraband of war. The foregoing is hereby made known for the information und observance of all concerned. The Ministry of Finances, Copenhagen, the 30th of June 1861. FENGER. L. Petersen.

CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. FRIDAY, 4tii OCTOBER, 1SG1. TIIU WHITHER. On Wednesday morning the weather presented a very threatening appearance. The barometer, although falling, did not however indicate a gale ; and that circumstance inspired us with hope. Early iu the morning the rain began to fall, accompanied with lightning and continuous peals of thunder. The electrical discharges iu the atmosphere were terrific; just such weather as would have delighted Crosse, the Electrician. The fall of rain was general over the Island; some places, however, registering more lines than others. In this town about thirty lines fell. In West End the sea roso in heavy waves which broke in violence on the shore. One small craft, in attempting to put to sea, was thrown ashore ; and the Schooner Rosaline, having but two boys onboard at tbo time, would most probably have shared the same fate, but for tbc intrepid conduct of Capt. Thomas Smith, who, at great risk of his life, ventured to goon board accompanied by a few fishermen. The boat in which they left the shore was overturned and immediately dashed to pieces. Capt. Smith and his men had a narrow escape iu attempting to swim ashore ; all however reached safely. They immediately made another attempt, and, although the boat received some injury, they got onboard the Schooner in time to save her by putting immediately to sea, a feat of no little difficulty with a heavy sea and the wind blowing in shore. The Rosaline came to anchor in this harbour about 5 þÿo clock in the afternoon.

The debates in the Colonial Council that we publish to-day, anil the recent election at Christiansted of a member for the Burgher Council, that terminated

S f « P R n 1 I & H \ in the laudable re-election of its Chairman, are subjects possessing interest even for the inhabitants of St. Thomas, as they are well calculated to explode those statements which it is the aim and wish of extreme conservatives in Copenhagen and their co-adjutors of these Islands to have circulated, that supreme indifference is manifested by the Colonists in all that relates to themselves. Never was there a more erroneous impression attempted to he raised than this same one of apathy on the part of these communities regarding the modes of Administration. If there has been apathy at all, it results from the clear perception and consequent conviction of the- inhabitants that the representative systems, as ordained for these Islands, were so devoid of any control by them, that in preference to being made the mediums of carrying out measures, ofttimes not in the best interests of the Islands, it was better not to participate in them at till. Evidence the address of the Honorable II. L. Arnesen to his Constituents, and the action of our own Burgher Council, respecting its dimission. And the supreme Government may feel assured that whenever a Legislative system, with the elements of selfgovernment, is introduced for these Islands, their inhabitants will shew themselves as fully alive to the benefits resulting therefrom as could he found anywhere else, whatever the Berlingske Tiilende to the contrary may labour to propound. A close reading of the proceedings of the Colonial Council, above

referred to, will disclose some very singular reasoning; tor instance, it is maintained that so long as there continues a deficiency in the Budget of St. Croix, so long there should he withheld tiny step towards self-government; now if this could he maintained as conclusive reasoning for St. Croix, what then, we might ask, ought to have been the form of Government that St. Thomas should long since have possessed, since it is acknowledged that t his Island has, for all time, been in excess of receipt over expenditure. Certainly on that hypothesis it ought to have been the most self-governing Island on the globe. However, we do most sincerely trust, that what is now transpiring in St. Croix, and which may he very well taken as a reflex of public opinion in St. Thomas, will serve to annul in the future whatever extreme conservatives on all sides may feel anxious to assert in regard to indifference on the part of these Colonies respecting self-government.

The 2ud question on tlic Order of the day was the 2nd discussion of the draft of a law to effect a separation of the revenue of the island of St. Croix from the finances of the Mothercountry. Two amendments were proposed ; the first jointly by the 5th member t r Christiansted (Rothe) and the 3rd crown member (Stnkcmann) was as follows : " That the Council, instead of iho contained in the draft voted : That the Colonial Council address, to His Majesty the King, a inu.-t submissive petition, that it bo tak n under consideration in what manner a separation of t Iio finances of the Colonies from those of the M>thercouDtry can be t fleeted and that the results of the investigations for this purpose as well as a draft based thereon be laid before the Colonial Council in its ordinary or an extraordinarysession next year. The 5th member for Clnistiansted (Rothe) recommended the amendment principally on the ground of the finances of St. Croix having, as explained by the Government, showed a deficit for the last years, and because lie did not think the Council in possession of the information required to form a correct opinion as to the best manner in which the separation, so much to be desired, ought to be effected. The Council would, by adopting the draft of the 5 members and opposing all the measures of the Governor, only contribute to weaken his position, which on the contrary it ought to Lc our

wish to sco strengthened if we desired to sec measures carried that were desirable. The Governor said, that according to all ho had stated, during the previous discussion on the present Draft, regarding the impossibility of carrying it through, ho must declare himself in favor of the amendment proposed by the two members ; it had afforded liirn pleasure to see this amendment proposed by them, as this plainly showed, that the difference of opinion which had been so strongly apparent during the previous discussion of this question, was chiefly with regard to the manner or form in which the petition from the Colonial Council ought to he made, while we all agreed in the main point, Damely the desire of a separation of the islands' finances from those of the Mothcrcountry. If the amendments were adopted, reference might in the Report of the Council on the Draft of the Budget, bo made to them, nnd he would consider it desirable that an opportunity was in this manner offered for obtaining an expression of opinion on the question during the approaching sitting of tho Imperial Council, and which it would be of interest to be acquainted with beforo the matter was pushed fui tlier here. But lio must observe, that the style and tone adopted in the Committee's report on the Budget with regard to the subject under discussion and in general was far fiotu being adopted to call forth a favorable opinion of the colony or its representation in the legislative Assemblies in the Mothcrcountry. mittee's report must give the idea, that the colonics were hero looked upon as wronged in their financial relations to the Mothcrcountry, whereas he had proved from the State- Accounts, that the Statetreasury's expenses, especially for St. Croix, have for a series of years considerably exceeded tho revenues from the island ; and yet the State-Accounts had not included any contribution from the colonics towards the common expenses of the State ex-

They seem hardly to have comprehended their own triumph, and, t hough it was easy to ascribe their caution to political considerations, it docs not appear that such motives could really have influenced their decisions. On the contrary, instead of refraining from an attack on the capital, they seem to have been gradually working up to that very point, and to have made till their calculations for an advance into Maryland, and a seizure of the Federal metropolis. Perhaps we shall best explain their delay by attributing it to a deficiency in the material of war. They are said to be very weak in artillery and very ill-provided with ammunition. Otherwise, notwithstanding the relative inferiority of their resources, they would probably have been strong enough to march upon Washington before the North had time to recover itself. In the first place what reason have wo for looking on this as a war waged agaiust slavery ? Wc must judge the movement by thoso who lead and speak for it. Wo could not forget the startling lesson taught us by the tcsulU of the war in Kanzas. There wc saw, as we supposed, the battle between slavery and freedom being fought out with the bowie knife and the rifle. We abhorred the ruffians who sought to thrust slavery upon that hitherto untainted soil. We sympathized deeply with those who gallantly fought for freedom. At length right triumphed over wrong. Could we help perceiving, after that, that the strugglo between þÿ free þÿsoil and þÿ slavoþÿsoil was mainly a struggle for Northern or Southern votes and supremacy in Congress and tho Senate; partly, too, a Protectionist struggle of tho white labourer against the competition of the onslaved negro ? But we were driven to look with somewhat guarded enthusiasm on recent events after catching such a broad glimpse of these not dishonourable, hut not sublime motives. (Tlie Barbados West Indian, November 26, 1861.) THE OUTRAGE ON BOARD THE TRENT. At Martinique this affair lias created quite as much excitement as in the British Colonies. How, nsks the Antilles, has this act of unheard-of audacity been committed ? What circumstances have fatally induced the Captain of the Trent to suffer this most flagrant outrage to he inflicted on the flag of his country ? He describes the act as þÿfollows On " the 9th instant Messrs. Slidell and Mason took passage in I he Trent, Cnpt. Moir, leaving Havanna in the morning. Scarcely an hour after her departure, a few miles from the port, and almost in the Spanish waters, the Steam-Corvette San Jacinto hove in sight, which was cruising along the coast, and suddenly the federal vessel stood across the Trent, hoisted colors to show she was going to fire on her, cleared the decks, run out her guns, got ready her men to hoard, and gave notice to the English ship to stop and await her visit. The Trent, astonished a.t this order, and still more at these hostile demonstrations, obeyed at once. Soon afterwards she was approached by two boats armed with swivels, and 60 men, sword in hand, with revolvers at their side, rushed on deck The chief of this band summoned

t d-1 d B K A it $ the Captain of the Steamer to deliver up to him the list of his passengers and the hooks of the ship, which might assist in examining the list, so as to satisfy himself if amongst the passengers were the self-styled Commissioners of the Confederate States, Messrs. Slidell and Mason, who were claimed as rebels and traitors by the Government of the United States. Round Capt. Moir, overcome with indignation easy to understand, were ranged the Officers of the Treiit, behind him stood a group of stupefied passengers, in front the mates could with difficulty restrain t he exasperated sailors; but all this crowd of unarmed persons, surprised in their security and confidence, were kept in awe by the force of men who bad seized the deck, and by the San Jacinto lying within a few yards motionless, with her guns pointed. What a sight! What a variety of emotions must have passed through the hearts of these travellers of every nation accustomed to respect the rights of nations, and who in some sort repre sentcd at this moment outraged humanity. The captain of the Trent, it can easily be imagined, repelled with indignation the demand which tlu-y dared to make to him, and protested with energy against the acts of which he was the victim. But in vain his refusal ; useless his protest ; Ihe order is given to search everywhere, and after a search which respects nothing, they declare the presence on board of Messrs. Slidell and M a son, their families and secretaries. Captain Moir is again sum-

moned to deliver up these traitors, under penalty, if he refused, of the most serious consequences lo him, his passengers, and ship. Again, a refusal and another protest, followed by a renewed search, which every moment threatens to end worse. A little more and they must come to force. Then Messrs. Slidell, Mason, and their Secretaries, leaving the silent row of the passengers, amongst whom they remained till then, advanced with calmness and dignity towards the American Officer, gave their names, acknowledged themselves, and delivered themselves up prisoners voluntarily to avoid the effusion of blood and the worst evils. Noble and generous conduct þÿ which touched every heart, except tiiose who ought to have been the first to feel it. In vain Captain Motn renews his protests ; in vain generous passengers make solemn appeals to the right of nations, to the inviolable respect due to a friendly flag ; in vain they call upon them to remember that the deck of a ship covered by the British Ensign was the same as the land of England, that sacred soil, proud and jealous of its rights, which lately refused to give up an accomplice in an attempt upon the þÿ Europe; in vain, the Commissioners first crown head of of the Confederate States are seized, bound, (garottes,) it is said, and dragged away by the American sailors. Just as they were about to quit the deck of the Trent, a crueller scene than any which had taken place revived the the sympathies of the passengers, the

wives and children of those amongst them who had their families with them, threw themselves amongst the ranks of the federalists and demanded, overwhelmed with grief and tears, to share in the lot of a husband whom they would not quit, of a beloved father around whom they cling sobbing. They are pitilessly torn away, pushed back, and the Federalists, after having as a last adie", cried out, " we dont want the

women and children," descend into their boats and return to the San Jacinto, which started away with all the speed she could. Three days afterwards the Trent anchored at St. Thomas, and the whole city could read this account of the only maritime expedition of the Northern States in the Carribean Sen " The Antilles concludes: þÿ "One word more: the insult above described is not the only one which England lias to avenge. One of lite Northern ships blockading the Missisippi lias fired on an English frigate, under pretext that she showed a disposition to transgress the limits of the blockade; and the last news from New York tell of a controversy which has arisen, on the arrest of British subjects, between Ihe Secretary of State at Washington and Lord Lyons, the British .Minister. A p ro t est of the latter had been placed in the hands of Air Seward, who answered arrogantly enough, 1 hat everybody must submit to measures rendered necessary tor the public safety. Wait a little, and we shall see what John Bon, will say to Brother Jonathan, now that lie is no longer Prime Minister of King Cotton.
